Human behavior is multimodal and dynamic in nature. From the precise integration of visual, somatosensory and vestibular information when walking [@mackinnonSensorimotorAnatomyGait2018], to the effortless coordination of speech, gestures and facial expressions when communicating [@hollerMultimodalLanguageProcessing2019], our actions continuously unfold through multiple sensory, haptic and motor signals that interact across time and space. Yet, researchers investigating different aspects of human behavior in the context of psychological and neurocognitive sciences have traditionally relied on temporally coarse-grained, unimodal measures: e.g., capturing only one type of signal at a time, often through indirect proxies such as self-report questionnaires [@baumeisterPsychologyScienceSelfReports2007], button presses, or accuracy scores [@maselliSimpleLaboratoryStudies2023; @parsonsPsychologicalScienceNeeds2019].
	
In recent years, however, the research landscape in cognitive science has changed dramatically. Technological and methodological advancements in sensing equipment, recording devices and computational tools that handle high-dimensional data have paved the way for a new era of behavioral research, moving several interdisciplinary fields from unimodal to multimodal approaches [e.g. see @turkMultimodalInteractionReview2014; @yangReviewMultimodalityResearch2019 for reviews]. In the last decade alone, more than sixty thousand scientific publications within social sciences have appeared with the term “multimodal” in their keywords, marking a 400% increase from the previous decade (based on a Scopus keyword search conducted in 2025). In contrast to the past, where measurements were limited to either unimodal proxies or laborious manual labelling of observed behaviors [e.g. @brugmanAnnotatingMultimediaMultimodal], nowadays researchers can employ high-frequency sensing devices to simultaneously capture movements, speech, physiological changes, gaze patterns, and even neural states, as they unfold in real time. For instance, optical motion tracking systems such as OptiTrack [@nagymateApplicationOptiTrackMotion2018] can be combined with wearable eye trackers [@gunawardenaEyetrackingTechnologiesMobile2022] and electrophysiological recordings [@moonWearableMultimodalWireless2023] to study complex intra- and inter-personal brain-behavior dynamics of phenomena such as neural synchrony [e.g. @koulSpontaneousDyadicBehavior2023], cognitive workload [e.g. @charlesMeasuringMentalWorkload2019] or psychosocial stress [e.g. @richerMachineLearningbasedDetection2024]. Accordingly, the progress in technological infrastructures has enabled a similar progress in the level of spatio-temporal granularity with which researchers can ask and answer questions about different neuro-cognitive-behavioral phenomena [@laudanskaDataDiscoveryTechnology2025].

Despite these technological advancements, there are important methodological challenges that will shape the future directions of this emerging field. To start, building a functioning multimodal laboratory from scratch can be both technically complex and prohibitively costly for many researchers. Firstly, one needs to select the appropriate recording system for each modality, a choice that can be particularly overwhelming given the sheer number of different manufacturers, pricing ranges and technical specifications. For instance, there are currently dozens of commercially available motion tracking (MT) systems, spanning a wide range of technologies – from high-precision optical systems (e.g. Vicon, Qualisys, Optitrack) to wearable inertial sensors (e.g., Xsen, Noraxon), to markerless computer vision tools (e.g. OpenPose, MediaPipe) – and costing from few hundred, to hundreds of thousands euros [for a comprehensive review, see @juveriyahComprehensiveSurveyHuman2023]. Secondly, assembling all multiple recording devices (MT, microphones, physiological sensors, etc.) in a spatially efficient and modular setup without interfering with participants' natural behaviors presents design and logistical challenges. For instance, many commercially available setups are only tailored to fixed laboratory environments, rely on heavy infrastructure, and are primarily designed for single-participant recordings, making them difficult to relocate or adapt the laboratory to real-world settings and/or multiple participants [@ladouceUnderstandingMindsRealWorld2017; @maselliSimpleLaboratoryStudies2023]. Thirdly, a major challenge lies in integrating and synchronizing the heterogeneous data streams that all of these recording devices produce. In fact, each modality (whether MT, audio, gaze or physiology) is sampled at different rates (e.g., ranging from 60 Hz for videos to 16 kHz for audio), recorded using different hardware and software, and encoded in different formats [@vieiraSynchronizationMultimodalPhysiological2026].  Ensuring that all these signals are temporally aligned with sufficient precision and stored in an integrated and accessible format is non-trivial, especially in studies involving many recording devices in highly naturalistic paradigms with multiple interacting participants. Finally, even after data collection, researchers are faced with the substantial demands of managing and analyzing multi-dimensional, time-varying datasets (such as dozens of 2D video streams, high-resolution audio, and continuous physiological signals) all of which need to be pre-processed, and organized for analysis. Without standardized pipelines or centralized data structures, this process can become fragmented and error-prone, especially when integrating data from multiple participants or sessions. 

In most cases, researchers have outsourced these challenges to proprietary companies that manufacture recording systems with accompanied blackboxed software, with further help from technical support staff in the case of high-resourced institutions. To capture participants movements, one might indeed conveniently opt for a state-of-the-art MT system from a proprietary company that usually offers extensive customer support (including installation), optimal recording accuracy, and a user-friendly software with built-in analyses packages [@merriauxStudyViconSystem2017; @vanderkrukAccuracyHumanMotion2018]. While these proprietary solutions offer clear advantages, they also come with some important drawbacks: they are often prohibitively expensive (e.g. Qualisys: circa 150-200K €, Vicon: 200-250K €), relying on closed-sourced software and analyses toolkits, often with monthly subscription costs [@vanschaikMotionTrackingDevelopmental2020]. As a result, they are not accessible to many researchers or institutions working with limited budgets (e.g., in low-middle income countries), nor easily adaptable for use in non-standard experimental setups or in field-based research. Additionally, even when the budget allows, the issue of data integration and synchronization across different devices (e.g., an MT system with physiological sensors) still remains, as each proprietary device (typically) operates within closed device/software ecosystems that can make cross-platform integration challenging at many levels.  

Given this context, a central question within the field of multimodal research is: how much should we rely on these proprietary systems, and how much should we instead invest in building intellectual capital toward more affordable, open-source alternatives? Beyond the drawbacks outlined above, an exclusive reliance on proprietary commercial systems can also hinder the sharing of knowledge required to build and operate multimodal setups, which risks being locked behind licenses, paywalled documentation, or the institutional memory of well-funded labs. Therefore, we believe that investing in alternatives can help democratize access to multimodal research and foster a more equitable and collaborative scientific ecosystem, where researchers engage in open pedagogical practices and actively contribute to the development, adaptation, and dissemination of methodological tools [@woelfleOpenScienceResearch2011]. 
	
With this in mind, here we introduce the Mobile Multimodal Laboratory (MMLab). The MMLab project provides an affordable, open-source solution to anyone interested in capturing multimodal human behaviors in both controlled and ecological environments. It comprises a suite of freely available resources – i.e., the present paper, a detailed Quarto manual and a comprehensive coding repository – specifically designed to guide users through all the steps entailed in building a fully functional mobile multimodal lab, including synchronizing, recording, and analysing data streams of interest. The MMLab was built around the following key features:  

- Accessibility: all documentation, code, and tutorials are open sourced to ensure broad accessibility, transparency, and reuse across research communities.
- Affordability: the proposed setup (video recording optimized for 3D motion tracking, audio-recording, and physiological signals from two participants) can be fully assembled for under 10,000€, as it relies on low-cost components and, whenever possible, non-proprietary hardware and software.
- Portability: MMLab is designed to be compact and easily transportable, allowing researchers to use it in a range of testing environments beyond traditional lab spaces.
- Built-in Integration and Synchronization: data from each recording device is centrally integrated through the Lab Streaming Layer [LSL, @kotheLabStreamingLayer2025], which allows for precise temporal synchronization of multimodal streams at the level of recording.
- Modularity: the setup supports a wide range of interchangeable components and sensors compatible with LSL, allowing researchers to customize the lab to suit specific research goals.
Community-maintenance: MMLab aims to gather researchers interested in expanding and maintaining the current infrastructure to ensure longevity of the project, solve common troubleshooting issues, or implement demands from the community. 

::: {.content-visible when-format="doc"}
The present paper serves both as an introductory guide and a step-by-step tutorial designed to walk researchers and technical staff through the process of assembling and operating the MMLab. Alongside the manuscript, we also provide an online manual available at https://multimoblab.github.io/Mobile-Multimodal-Lab/ . The online manual is an extended copy of this manuscript: it provides additional technical details and more in-depth explanations of scripts that enable implementations of all steps. Unlike this manuscript, it is meant to be regularly updated to resolve issues, implement technological innovations,  or accommodate wishes of MMLab users.
:::

To illustrate each step of the MMLab, we grounded our guide in a proof-of-concept experiment in which two participants engaged in an interpersonal singing task while being simultaneously recorded across multiple 2D video streams (e.g., for 3D motion tracking), high-frequency microphones (e.g. for prosodic or semantic analyses) and wireless physiological sensors capturing electrocardiogram (ECG), electromyography (EMG) and respiration cycles. All these heterogeneous data streams were time-synchronized using the LSL system [@kotheLabStreamingLayer2025], an open-source middleware that allows centralized data collection with sub-millisecond synchronization. Our toolkit further offers scripts to handle data integration and processing, and example analysis. This proof-of-concept experimental configuration is intended as the default setup that can be adapted to meet individual research needs and evolving technological capabilities. Other recording devices (e.g. EEG or eye-tracking) can easily be incorporated into the pipeline, provided they are compatible with the LSL.
In the following methods section, we provide a detailed guide on how to (1) set up, (2) preprocess, (3) process, and (4) analyze the multimodal data recorded with the MMLab setup, grounding these procedures in our (0) proof-of-concept experiment. The methods section is structured into five main parts:

0. The Proof-of-Concept Experiment: This part describes the rationale behind our (0.1) experimental paradigm (a structured interpersonal singing task) and (0.2)  details of the experimental design and manipulations. 

1. Setup of the MMLab: This part outlines the specific hardware and software components used in our MMLab, detailing the rationale for choosing our equipment, the steps involved in assembling the components, and the recording procedures for each modality. Specifically, we describe the setup for video recording optimized for 3D motion tracking (1.1), high-fidelity audio recording (1.2), wireless physiological recordings of electrocardiogram (ECG), electromyography (EMG) and respiration (1.3), and the integration and synchronization of all data streams via the Lab Streaming Layer (1.4).

2. Preprocessing of Multimodal Data: This part details all the steps required to prepare the recorded multimodal data for analysis. Based on our analyses scripts, we describe the procedures for extracting and converting individual streams from the unified recording file (2.1), segmenting each stream based on shared LSL timestamps of experimentally relevant events (2.2), clipping the externally stored raw videos to match the corresponding LSL time segments (2.3), and merging the clipped videos with their synchronized audio recordings (2.4).

3. Multimodal Signal Processing: This part details the extraction and filtering of relevant signals from each multimodal time series. We first describe the full motion tracking pipeline (3.1), covering the selection of pose estimation algorithm (3.1.1), video preparation (3.1.2), camera calibration (3.1.3), and 2D and 3D pose estimation via FreeMoCap (3.1.4). We then describe the signal processing procedures for the remaining modalities (3.2), including the extraction of audio amplitude envelopes (3.2.1), ECG filtering (3.2.2), muscle activation envelopes from EMG (3.2.3), and respiratory waveforms (3.2.4). Finally, we describe how all processed signals are resampled, temporally aligned, and merged into a single multimodal matrix per trial (3.3).

4. Multimodal Analyses: This part presents a proof-of-concept analysis pipeline using mutual information (MI) to quantify interpersonal coupling across modalities and experimental conditions. We describe the signal normalization procedures (4.1) and the MI analysis framework (4.2), including time-lagged and sliding-window computations across all between-participant signal pairs.
